name: Yangshao, Longshan & Erlitou (Xia)
summary: From Liangzhu’s jade cong and massive hydraulic dams in the Yangtze delta to Longshan black pottery and the Bronze Age palace-workshops at Erlitou (linked by archaeologists to the traditional Xia Dynasty).
keyFacts: Liangzhu hydraulic dam complex (3000 BCE)—oldest large-scale water engineering in East Asia
Piece-mold ritual bronze vessels, silk sericulture, and rammed-earth palaces at Erlitou

name: Shang Dynasty
summary: First archaeologically verified Chinese dynasty with contemporary written records: over 150,000 oracle bone inscriptions (jiaguwen) directly ancestral to modern Chinese characters, alongside monumental bronze casting (Houmuwu ding) and Sanxingdui in Sichuan.
keyFacts: Oracle Bone Script (Jiaguwen)—direct ancestor of modern Chinese writing used for 3,300+ years
832 kg Houmuwu Ding bronze vessel & Tomb of Lady Fu Hao

name: Zhou Dynasty (Spring & Autumn / Warring States)
summary: China’s longest-lasting dynasty (825 years). Articulated the "Mandate of Heaven" (Tianming) and during its Eastern Zhou era (Spring & Autumn and Warring States) witnessed cast-iron metallurgy, the crossbow, Dujiangyan irrigation, and the Hundred Schools of Thought.
keyFacts: Mandate of Heaven political philosophy & Book of Songs (Shijing)
Confucius (Analects), Laozi (Dao De Jing), and Sun Tzu (The Art of War)
Blast-furnace cast iron (centuries before Europe), crossbow, and Dujiangyan irrigation system (256 BCE, still irrigating Sichuan today)

name: Qin & Han Dynasties
summary: Qin Shi Huang unified the Warring States in 221 BCE, standardizing script, weights, coins, and road gauges and building the Terracotta Army and early Great Wall. The succeeding 400-year Han Dynasty institutionalized Confucian education, opened the Silk Road, and invented paper and the seismometer.
keyFacts: Unification of Chinese script, Terracotta Army, and Imperial Civil Service Imperial University
Invention of papermaking by Cai Lun (105 CE) & Zhang Heng’s seismoscope (132 CE)
Sima Qian’s Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji) & opening of the Silk Road
evidence: Bibliography pointers only. The cited pages were not opened for this row.

name: Sui, Tang & Song Dynasties
summary: After the Sui built the 1,776 km Grand Canal, Cosmopolitan Tang Chang’an became the world’s largest city and golden age of poetry (Li Bai, Du Fu). The succeeding Song Dynasty achieved a proto-industrial revolution: woodblock and movable-type printing, gunpowder, the magnetic mariner’s compass, paper currency (Jiaozi), and coal-fired steel production.
keyFacts: Three of the "Four Great Inventions": Woodblock/Movable-Type Printing (Bi Sheng, 1040), Gunpowder, and Magnetic Compass
Grand Canal (longest artificial waterway in the world) & world’s first government paper money
Competitive imperial civil service examinations (Keju) & Tang poetry

name: Ming & Qing Dynasties → Modern China
summary: The Ming Dynasty built the Forbidden City, the stone-clad Ming Great Wall, blue-and-white Jingdezhen porcelain, and launched Admiral Zheng He’s 300-ship treasure fleets across the Indian Ocean to East Africa (1405–1433). The Qing expanded China’s frontiers before the 1911 Xinhai Revolution and China’s late-20th/21st-century economic and technological resurgence.
keyFacts: Forbidden City, Ming Great Wall, Yongle Encyclopedia, and Zheng He’s 7 Indian Ocean voyages
